## Passages for Questions 7-12

**Passage: "Industrial Shadows" (Historical Fiction)**

The factory whistle pierced the dawn over Pittsburgh's steel district. Samuel wiped the sleep from his eyes and reached for his lunch pail—another day in the Andrew Carnegie Steel Works. At seventeen, he had worked the rail mills for two years, long enough to know that ambition was a luxury for men who didn't have families depending on every dollar.

The foreman's voice cut through the machinery's roar: "Thompson line, full speed ahead!" Samuel felt the familiar tension in his shoulders as the glowing steel bars emerged from the rollers. His father had lost three fingers to these same machines before the company declared him unfit for work. Samuel had promised himself he would find another way out—but there was no other work for boys from the Hill District, not real work that paid enough to survive.

## Passages for Questions 13-18

**Passage: "The Whale's Call" (Literary Fiction)**

Captain Ahab never spoke about the白鲸—that white whale—except in the darkest hours of the night watch. I had heard the stories from the first mate, a man from Maine who had been on three previous voyages with Ahab and survived each one. "The captain's leg is oak," he told me once, "but his mind is the sea itself. It only rests when Moby-Dick is beneath the hull."

I was just a cabin boy, barely seventeen, and I didn't understand what drove a man to chase a single creature across five oceans. But I understood the crew's fear—the way they whispered when Ahab's shadow fell across the deck, the way they avoided his eyes during dinner. The whale had taken his leg; we all knew it was only a matter of time before it took more.

## Passages for Questions 7-12

**Passage: "The Forgotten Frontier: Solar Energy in the American Southwest" (History/Social Studies)**

In 1973, architect Edward L. R. D. "Ed"Mazria began experimenting with passive solar design in Santa Fe, New Mexico. His goal was simple: design buildings that captured winter sunlight for heating while using strategic overhangs to provide shade in summer. The results were groundbreaking—a home in Los Alamos achieved 80% of its heating from the sun alone, using no mechanical systems whatsoever.

Despite these early successes, solar energy remained largely marginal throughout the 1970s and 1980s. The oil crises of the era prompted temporary interest, but cheap fossil fuels quickly reasserted their dominance. "The industry was always one price shock away from relevance," notes energy historian Dr. Maria Santos of Arizona State University. "When oil dropped to $10 per barrel in 1986, thousands of solar contractors went out of business overnight."

Only in the past decade has solar experienced a true renaissance, driven by plummeting panel costs and federal tax incentives. Arizona now generates more solar energy per capita than any other state, while California's ambitious mandate requires all new homes to include solar systems starting 2020.

## Passages for Questions 13-18

**Passage: "The Social Media Paradox: Connection or Isolation?" (Psychology/Sociology)**

A landmark study published in the Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology examined the relationship between social media use and mental health among 143 college students in Oregon. Participants were divided into two groups: one limited to 30 minutes daily on Instagram, Facebook, or TikTok; the other continued normal usage. After three weeks, the limited-use group reported significant reductions in loneliness and depression compared to the control group.

Lead researcher Dr. Melissa C. Holloway explains: "We found that passive scrolling—simply viewing others' content without interacting—was most strongly associated with negative outcomes. Active engagement, such as messaging friends directly, showed neutral or even positive effects."

However, some experts urge caution in interpreting these results. Dr. James Okafor of Stanford University argues: "Three weeks is far too short to draw meaningful conclusions about mental health impacts. We need longitudinal studies tracking users over years, not weeks." He also notes that correlation does not imply causation—people struggling with depression may simply be more drawn to passive social media use.

## Questions 9-16: Dual Passages on Artificial Intelligence

**Passage A: "Artificial Intelligence in the Classroom" (Education)**

The integration of AI tools like ChatGPT into American classrooms presents both opportunities and challenges. In the Los Angeles Unified School District, some teachers have embraced AI as a personalized tutoring companion, noting that struggling students who previously hesitated to ask questions now engage freely with chatbots. "It never judges, never tires, and can explain concepts twenty different ways until understanding clicks," says math teacher Roberto Hernandez.

However, concerns about academic integrity have followed. The College Board, which administers the SAT, has updated its testing protocols to detect AI-generated essays. In response to cheating concerns, some universities—including the University of Michigan—now require proctored examinations for all written assessments. Critics argue this represents an expensive arms race that diverts resources from actual learning.

**Passage B: "The AI Writing Debate" (Technology)**

The question of whether AI-generated text constitutes genuine thinking has sparked fierce philosophical debate. Dr. Patricia Walls, a cognitive scientist at MIT, argues: "Language models don't understand meaning—they predict patterns. A chatbot describing grief sounds like grief, but there's no actual emotional experience behind it." This view suggests that using AI for writing assignments is fundamentally dishonest.

On the other side, philosopher Dr. James Oduya of Stanford counters: "Humans have always used tools to augment thinking—from the abacus to spell-check. AI is simply the next iteration. The question isn't whether AI writes, but how it changes what it means to be a writer." This perspective implies that adapting to AI is not cheating but evolution.
